questions.q: Pollen grains of wind-pollinated flowers are generally:
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers have light, non-sticky pollen that is easily carried by air currents.

questions.q: The seed coat develops from which part of the ovule?
questions.explanation: The integuments of the ovule harden to form the protective seed coat.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of insect-pollinated flowers?
options: Small and dull with a feathery stigma
Large, colourful and scented, with sticky pollen
questions.explanation: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects with colour, fragrance and nectar, and their pollen is sticky.

questions.q: The filiform apparatus, which guides the entry of the pollen tube, is present in the:
questions.explanation: The synergids have special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip called the filiform apparatus.

questions.q: Which of the following prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy?
questions.explanation: In dioecious plants such as papaya, male and female flowers are on different plants, so neither self-pollination nor pollination between flowers of the same plant can occur.

questions.q: How many pollen mother cells must undergo meiosis to produce 100 pollen grains?
questions.explanation: Each pollen mother cell gives a tetrad of four pollen grains, so 100/4 = 25 cells are needed.

questions.q: Define pollination and name its three types based on the source of pollen.
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. Based on the source it is autogamy (same flower), geitonogamy (a different flower of the same plant) and xenogamy (a flower of a different plant).
keyPoints: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
questions.explanation: Only xenogamy brings genetically different pollen.

questions.q: Why would apomixis in hybrid crop varieties be of great use to farmers?
questions.answer: Seeds of hybrids segregate in the next generation, so farmers must buy fresh hybrid seeds every year. If a hybrid is made apomictic, its seeds do not segregate and keep the hybrid characters, so farmers can use the same seeds for years, reducing the cost of seed.
keyPoints: Hybrid seeds segregate and lose characters
Apomictic seeds are clones of the hybrid
Farmers can reuse seeds, reducing cost
questions.explanation: Apomixis is an area of active research for hybrid seed production.

questions.q: The inner glandular lining of the human uterus is called the:
questions.explanation: The uterine wall has three layers: the outer perimetrium, middle myometrium and inner endometrium.

questions.q: The loose fold of skin that covers the glans penis is called the:
questions.explanation: The glans penis is covered by a loose fold of skin called the foreskin.

questions.q: The cervical canal together with the vagina forms the:
questions.explanation: The cavity of the cervix, called the cervical canal, and the vagina form the birth canal.

questions.q: The finger-like fimbriae at the end of the fallopian tube help in:
options: Collection of the ovum after ovulation
questions.explanation: Fimbriae are close to the ovary and help to collect the ovum released at ovulation.

questions.q: Home pregnancy test kits are based on the detection of which hormone in the urine?
questions.explanation: hCG is produced by the placenta only during pregnancy, so its presence indicates pregnancy.

questions.q: In human males, FSH acts on which cells to stimulate the process of spermiogenesis?
questions.explanation: FSH acts on the Sertoli cells and stimulates secretion of factors that help in spermiogenesis; LH acts on Leydig cells.

questions.q: Name the three primary germ layers of the embryo and state that they form.
questions.answer: The three germ layers are the ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. They arise from the inner cell mass and give rise to all the tissues and organs of the body.
questions.explanation: The germ layers form after gastrulation.

questions.q: Explain how the hypothalamus and pituitary regulate spermatogenesis.
questions.answer: The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which acts on the anterior pituitary to secrete LH and FSH. LH acts on Leydig cells to secrete androgens, which stimulate spermatogenesis, and FSH acts on Sertoli cells to promote sperm formation.
keyPoints: LH acts on Leydig cells to release androgens
questions.explanation: Gonadotropins regulate the testes.

questions.q: Surgical sterilisation in the human female is called:
questions.explanation: In tubectomy the fallopian tubes are cut and tied, so the ovum cannot reach the uterus.

questions.q: Diseases or infections that are transmitted through sexual intercourse are collectively called:
questions.explanation: They are called STIs, venereal diseases (VD) or reproductive tract infections (RTI).

questions.q: Artificial insemination (AI) is useful for couples in which:
options: The husband has only a hormonal problem
The male partner cannot inseminate the female or has very low sperm counts in the ejaculate
questions.explanation: In AI, semen from the husband or a healthy donor is introduced into the vagina or uterus of the female.

questions.q: The rapid rise in the human population in the last century is mainly due to:
options: A decline in the death rate, maternal mortality and infant mortality
An increase in the death rate
A decrease in the birth rate
An increase in the sex ratio
questions.explanation: Better health facilities lowered the death rates while birth rates remained high.

questions.q: Oral contraceptive pills are usually taken daily for how many days, starting within the first five days of menstruation?
questions.explanation: The pill is taken for 21 days, followed by a gap of seven days, after which the course is repeated.

questions.q: The MTP Act was legalised with strict conditions mainly to:
options: Prevent its misuse, such as female foeticide
questions.explanation: The Act aims to allow abortion on legal grounds while checking its misuse.

questions.q: What is infertility? Mention two possible causes.
questions.answer: Infertility is the inability of a couple to produce children in spite of unprotected sexual cohabitation. The causes may be physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological, and either partner may be responsible.
keyPoints: Inability to conceive despite unprotected cohabitation
Causes: physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or psychological
questions.explanation: Infertility can be treated by assisted reproductive technologies.

questions.q: Why are condoms widely recommended as a contraceptive method?
questions.answer: Condoms are barriers made of thin rubber or latex that cover the penis (or vagina for female condoms), so they prevent sperms from entering the female tract. They also give protection from STIs including AIDS, are reversible, easy to use and have no side effects.
keyPoints: Reversible, easy to use, without side effects
questions.explanation: Condoms are the most widely used barrier method.

questions.q: In pea, round seed (R) is dominant over wrinkled seed (r). The genotype of a plant with wrinkled seeds is:
questions.explanation: A recessive trait appears only in the homozygous recessive condition, rr.

questions.q: Linkage and crossing over in Drosophila were studied in detail by:
questions.explanation: T. H. Morgan and his colleagues worked on linkage and recombination in fruit flies.

questions.q: In birds, the females have which sex chromosome constitution?
questions.explanation: In birds, females are heterogametic (ZW) and males are homogametic (ZZ).

questions.q: In the grasshopper, the male has:
questions.explanation: In the XO type of sex determination, males have only one X chromosome and females have two.

questions.q: In honeybees, the male drones are:
questions.explanation: Drones develop parthenogenetically from unfertilised eggs, so they are haploid, whereas queens and workers are diploid.

questions.q: A colour-blind man marries a woman who is a carrier. What proportion of their daughters is expected to be colour blind?
questions.explanation: XcY x XCXc gives daughters XCXc (carrier) and XcXc (colour blind) in equal numbers.

questions.q: What is non-disjunction? Name two disorders caused by it.
questions.answer: Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes or chromatids to separate during meiosis, so gametes with an extra or missing chromosome are formed. It causes aneuploidies like Down's syndrome (trisomy 21), Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY) and Turner's syndrome (XO).
keyPoints: Failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis
Gametes with extra or missing chromosomes
questions.explanation: Non-disjunction leads to aneuploidy.

questions.q: What is recombination? How is the frequency of recombination used in gene mapping?
questions.answer: Recombination is the formation of new combinations of genes by crossing over between homologous chromosomes. Morgan's student Sturtevant used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs as a measure of their distance on the chromosome and used it to prepare genetic maps.
keyPoints: New gene combinations by crossing over
Recombination frequency reflects distance between genes
Sturtevant used it to make genetic maps
questions.explanation: Genes that are far apart show more recombination.

questions.q: Transcription in bacteria is catalysed by:
questions.explanation: A single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyses transcription of all types of RNA in bacteria.

questions.q: The sugar present in DNA is:
questions.explanation: DNA contains the pentose sugar 2'-deoxyribose.

questions.q: The cellular site of protein synthesis is the:
questions.explanation: Translation occurs on ribosomes, which are made of rRNA and proteins.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the processing of hnRNA in eukaryotes?
options: Capping at the 5' end with methyl guanosine triphosphate and tailing at the 3' end with adenylate residues
Capping at the 3' end and tailing at the 5' end
Capping with adenine and tailing with guanine
Only splicing, with no capping or tailing
questions.explanation: After splicing, hnRNA receives a cap at the 5' end and a poly-A tail at the 3' end to become mRNA.

questions.q: In the lac operon, the y gene codes for:
questions.explanation: The z gene codes for beta-galactosidase, y for permease and a for transacetylase.

questions.q: The distance between two adjacent base pairs in DNA is 0.34 nm. What is the length of a DNA segment of 10^6 base pairs?
Differentiate between the template strand and the coding strand of DNA.
questions.answer: The template strand has the polarity 3' to 5' and is the strand copied by RNA polymerase to make RNA. The coding strand has the polarity 5' to 3' and its sequence is the same as the RNA, except that it has T in place of U.
keyPoints: Coding strand (5' to 3') has the same sequence as RNA except T for U
questions.explanation: The coding strand does not itself take part in transcription.

questions.q: Describe the three steps of translation.
questions.answer: In initiation, the ribosome subunits assemble on mRNA at the start codon AUG with the initiator tRNA. In elongation, tRNAs bring amino acids according to the codons and peptide bonds are formed. In termination, a stop codon is reached and the polypeptide is released.
questions.explanation: Release factors help at termination.

questions.q: Darwin's natural selection depends on the presence of:
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on heritable variations that give some individuals a better chance of survival and reproduction.

questions.q: According to the fossil evidence discussed in NCERT, Homo sapiens arose in:
questions.explanation: Homo sapiens arose in Africa and moved across continents, developing into distinct races.

questions.q: All vertebrate embryos develop a row of vestigial gill slits behind the head, but only fishes use them. This supports:
questions.explanation: Similar embryonic features point to descent from a common ancestor.

questions.q: The appearance of drug-resistant microbes and herbicide-resistant weeds is evidence of:
questions.explanation: Resistant forms are selected in the presence of the drug or herbicide and then increase in the population.

questions.q: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of allele A is 0.6. What is the frequency of the AA genotype?
questions.explanation: The frequency of AA is p squared = 0.6 x 0.6 = 0.36.

questions.q: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is maintained when:
options: The population is small and isolated
There is random mating with no selection, migration or mutation in a large population
questions.explanation: The principle holds only if allele frequencies are not changed by evolutionary forces.

questions.q: What is speciation? How can geographical isolation lead to it?
questions.answer: Speciation is the formation of a new species from an existing one. When a population is split by a geographical barrier, the groups cannot interbreed, and natural selection, mutation and drift act differently on them. In time they become reproductively isolated and form separate species.
questions.explanation: Darwin's finches are an example.

questions.q: Briefly trace the evolution of modern humans from early hominids.
questions.answer: Ape-like Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus were early primates. Australopithecus was an early hominid, followed by Homo habilis with a brain of 650-800 cc. Homo erectus had a brain of about 900 cc, Neanderthal man about 1400 cc, and Homo sapiens arose in Africa.
questions.explanation: Brain capacity generally increased through the series.

questions.q: The filarial worms that cause elephantiasis are transmitted by which mosquito?
questions.explanation: Culex mosquitoes transmit Wuchereria, the filarial worm.

questions.q: The examination of a thin slice of tissue under the microscope to detect cancer is called:
questions.explanation: A biopsy is the microscopic study of a sample of tissue after staining.

questions.q: Allergy is caused by:
options: An exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens called allergens
questions.explanation: Allergens such as dust and pollen trigger release of histamine from mast cells.

questions.q: Cannabinoids are obtained from:
questions.explanation: Cannabinoids are extracted from the inflorescences of Cannabis sativa; they affect the cardiovascular system.

questions.q: Cocaine, obtained from Erythroxylum coca, acts on the nervous system by interfering with the transport of the neurotransmitter:
questions.explanation: Cocaine interferes with dopamine transport, causing excessive stimulation.

questions.q: Rejection of a transplanted organ is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: T-lymphocytes recognise the graft as foreign and cause its rejection.

questions.q: State three measures to prevent vector-borne diseases such as malaria and dengue.
questions.answer: Avoid stagnating water, where mosquitoes breed, and keep surroundings clean. Use mosquito nets, repellents and screens, and spray insecticides in breeding places. Introduce larvivorous fish like Gambusia in ponds.
questions.explanation: Vector control is the main way of preventing these diseases.

questions.q: How is cancer detected and treated?
questions.answer: Cancer is detected by biopsy and histopathological study, by imaging such as radiography, CT and MRI, and by molecular tests for genes. Treatment includes surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy, and biological response modifiers such as alpha-interferon help the immune system to destroy tumours.
questions.explanation: Early detection improves the chance of a cure.

questions.q: Antibiotics are chemical substances produced by:
options: Certain microbes, which kill or retard the growth of other disease-causing microbes
questions.explanation: Antibiotics such as penicillin are made by microbes and act against other microbes.

questions.q: Which of the following is removed during primary treatment of sewage?
questions.explanation: Primary treatment is a physical process of filtration and sedimentation that removes floating material and grit.

questions.q: In biological control, ladybird beetles are used against:
questions.explanation: Ladybirds feed on aphids, and dragonflies feed on mosquitoes, so they are used as biocontrol agents.

questions.q: Trichoderma species are used as:
options: Biocontrol agents of several plant diseases
questions.explanation: Trichoderma are free-living fungi that are effective biocontrol agents of plant pathogens.

questions.q: Milk sets into curd faster in summer than in winter because:
options: Milk contains more fat in summer
Lactic acid bacteria grow and multiply faster at a warmer temperature
Sunlight converts lactose into lactic acid
questions.explanation: LAB need a suitable warm temperature to multiply and convert milk into curd.

questions.q: Using biofertilisers in place of chemical fertilisers mainly helps to:
options: Reduce chemical pollution and maintain soil fertility
questions.explanation: Biofertilisers enrich nutrients without the harmful effects of excess chemicals.

questions.q: Describe the role of microbes in making any two common household products.
questions.answer: Lactic acid bacteria convert milk into curd by producing lactic acid, which coagulates and digests milk proteins. The dough for idli and dosa is fermented by bacteria and baker's yeast ferments bread dough, producing CO2 that makes the dough rise.
keyPoints: Yeast produces CO2 that raises bread dough
questions.explanation: Fermentation by microbes is used in many foods.

questions.q: Why is it important to treat sewage before releasing it into rivers? Name one Indian action plan for this.
questions.answer: Untreated sewage contains organic matter and pathogens, which increase the BOD of rivers, reduce dissolved oxygen, harm aquatic life and spread disease. The Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan were launched to build sewage treatment plants and clean the rivers.
keyPoints: Sewage has high organic matter and pathogens
Raises BOD and harms aquatic life
questions.explanation: Treatment reduces water pollution.

questions.q: What is the first step in a recombinant DNA experiment?
questions.explanation: DNA must first be isolated in a pure form before it can be cut and joined.

questions.q: Which of the following is a commonly used bacterial host in cloning experiments?
questions.explanation: E. coli is the commonly used bacterial host for cloning.

questions.q: In the name of the cloning vector pBR322, the letters BR stand for:
options: Bolivar and Rodriguez, who developed it
questions.explanation: The p stands for plasmid, BR for the two scientists Bolivar and Rodriguez, and 322 is the number of the plasmid developed in their laboratory.

questions.q: In the isolation of DNA, RNA is removed by treating the extract with:
questions.explanation: Ribonuclease degrades RNA, protease removes proteins and lysozyme breaks bacterial cell walls.

questions.q: During agarose gel electrophoresis, which DNA fragments travel the farthest from the wells?
options: Fragments with the most A-T pairs
questions.explanation: The agarose gel acts as a sieve, so smaller fragments move faster and farther.

questions.q: For a human gene to be expressed in E. coli, it must be placed downstream of:
options: A promoter that functions in bacteria
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase of the host must recognise the promoter that controls the transcription of the inserted gene.

questions.q: Why can foreign DNA not easily enter a bacterial cell, and how is the host made competent?
questions.answer: DNA is a hydrophilic molecule and cannot pass through the cell membrane. The bacterial cells are treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium to increase the pores in the membrane, and then incubated with the recombinant DNA on ice, followed by a heat shock.
keyPoints: DNA is hydrophilic and cannot cross the membrane
questions.explanation: Other methods are microinjection and the gene gun.

questions.q: Explain how recombinant colonies are identified using the lacZ gene and a chromogenic substrate.
questions.answer: A foreign gene is inserted within the lacZ gene of the vector, which inactivates it. On a medium with a chromogenic substrate, non-recombinants have a functional beta-galactosidase and give blue colonies, while recombinants cannot make the enzyme and give colourless colonies.
questions.explanation: This is insertional inactivation.

questions.q: In the term Bt cotton, Bt stands for:
questions.explanation: Bt refers to Bacillus thuringiensis, the source of the toxin gene.

questions.q: Mature human insulin consists of:
options: A single polypeptide chain without disulphide bonds
Three chains A, B and C
Two polypeptide chains, A and B, linked by disulphide bridges
One chain with the C peptide
questions.explanation: In mature insulin the C peptide is removed, leaving chains A and B joined by disulphide bonds.

questions.q: PCR is also used to detect gene mutations in suspected:
questions.explanation: PCR helps to detect mutations in genes in suspected cancer patients.

questions.q: The first transgenic cow, which produced human alpha-lactalbumin in its milk, was named:
questions.explanation: Rosie was the first transgenic cow, born in 1997.

questions.q: Why is gene therapy of ADA deficiency by giving the patient genetically corrected lymphocytes not a permanent cure?
options: The gene is destroyed in lymphocytes at once
The lymphocytes are short-lived, so periodic infusions are needed
questions.explanation: A permanent cure would require introducing the gene into early embryonic marrow cells.

questions.q: In the first commercial production of human insulin, the A and B chains were linked together by:
questions.explanation: The separately produced chains were extracted and combined by creating disulphide bonds.

questions.q: What are transgenic bacteria? Give one example of a useful product.
questions.answer: Transgenic bacteria are bacteria that carry a foreign gene introduced by genetic engineering. For example, E. coli carrying the human insulin genes produces human insulin for diabetics.
keyPoints: Example: E. coli making human insulin
questions.explanation: Bacteria are easy to grow in large quantities.

questions.q: Describe how ELISA helps to diagnose an infection such as HIV.
questions.answer: ELISA works on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction. The patient's sample is added to a surface coated with antigen, and an enzyme-linked antibody detects bound antibodies, producing a colour change with a substrate. The colour shows that the person has been infected.
keyPoints: Enzyme-linked antibody gives a colour change
questions.explanation: Infection is detected by the presence of antibodies or antigens.

questions.q: The correct order of the ecological hierarchy from lower to higher level of organisation is:
questions.explanation: Organisms form populations, which make up communities, which together form biomes.

questions.q: Many plants flower in response to:
questions.explanation: Light and day length regulate flowering and other processes in plants and the behaviour of animals.

questions.q: The relationship between a fig tree and its pollinator wasp is an example of:
questions.explanation: The wasp pollinates the fig, and the fig provides the wasp with a place to lay eggs and food.

questions.q: Which of the following is an endoparasite?
questions.explanation: The liver fluke lives inside the host, whereas lice, ticks and leeches feed from outside.

questions.q: A pond of area 20 square metres has 600 water hyacinth plants. What is the density of the population per square metre?
questions.explanation: Density = 600/20 = 30 plants per square metre.

questions.q: In logistic growth, when the population size reaches the carrying capacity (K), the growth rate (dN/dt) becomes:
questions.explanation: At K the factor (K - N)/K becomes zero, so the population stops growing.

questions.q: How do organisms respond to high altitude, where oxygen is low?
questions.answer: At high altitude people may suffer from altitude sickness with nausea and fatigue. With time the body compensates by increasing red blood cell production, decreasing the binding capacity of haemoglobin and increasing the breathing rate.
questions.explanation: This is a physiological adaptation, called acclimatisation.

questions.q: Explain why parasites are usually host-specific and show special adaptations.
questions.answer: Parasites have co-evolved with their hosts, so they are adapted to the host's body conditions and defences and often cannot live in another host. They show loss of unnecessary sense organs, adhesive organs, high reproductive capacity and complex life cycles involving one or two hosts.
keyPoints: Loss of sense organs and adhesive organs
High reproductive capacity and complex life cycles
questions.explanation: Host specificity ensures that the parasite and host evolve together.

questions.q: Which of the following is a producer in an aquatic ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Phytoplankton photosynthesise and are the major producers of aquatic ecosystems.

questions.q: Which of the following is an aquatic ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic ecosystems.

questions.q: The conversion of ammonia to nitrate in the soil by bacteria such as Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter is called:
questions.explanation: Nitrosomonas converts ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate.

questions.q: Denitrification is the process of:
options: Conversion of nitrates into gaseous nitrogen
Release of ammonia from dead matter
questions.explanation: Bacteria such as Pseudomonas convert nitrate back to N2, which returns to the atmosphere.

questions.q: Although oceans cover most of the Earth's surface, their total productivity compared with that of land is:
questions.explanation: The oceans have a lower productivity than land because of limited light and nutrients, even though they are larger in area.

questions.q: The final stable community of a successional series, which is in near equilibrium with the environment, is called the:
questions.explanation: The climax community is stable, in equilibrium with the climate, and remains unchanged unless disturbed.

questions.q: What is stratification in a forest ecosystem?
questions.answer: Stratification is the vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels in an ecosystem. In a forest, trees occupy the top vertical layer or canopy, shrubs the second layer and herbs and grasses the bottom layer.
keyPoints: Trees, shrubs, then herbs and grasses
questions.explanation: Stratification reduces competition for light.

questions.q: Describe how carbon moves through the carbon cycle.
questions.answer: Producers fix atmospheric CO2 into organic matter by photosynthesis, and carbon passes to consumers through food chains. Carbon returns to the atmosphere through respiration, decomposition of dead matter and burning of fossil fuels and wood, and CO2 also exchanges with the oceans.
keyPoints: Released by respiration, decomposition and combustion
questions.explanation: The ocean is a large reservoir that exchanges carbon with the atmosphere.

questions.q: As per NCERT, how many of the world's biodiversity hotspots cover regions of India?
questions.explanation: Three hotspots, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and the Himalaya, cover India.

questions.q: Which of the following ecosystems has the greatest species diversity per unit area?
questions.explanation: Tropical rain forests like the Amazon have the highest species richness.

questions.q: Among the IUCN threat categories, which indicates the highest risk of extinction?
questions.explanation: Critically endangered species face an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild.

questions.q: Water hyacinth (Eichhornia) in Indian water bodies is regarded as:
questions.explanation: Water hyacinth, Lantana and Parthenium are invasive alien species that threaten native biodiversity.

questions.q: A tropical country near the equator such as Colombia has how many bird species compared with New York or Greenland, which are at higher latitudes?
questions.explanation: Species richness rises towards the equator, so the tropical country has far more bird species.

questions.q: Ex situ conservation is especially needed when:
options: The habitat is intact and stable
A species is so threatened that it needs protection outside its natural habitat
questions.explanation: Ex situ methods like zoos, gene banks and seed banks protect species that cannot survive in the wild.

questions.q: What is a keystone species? Give an example.
questions.answer: A keystone species is one whose presence has a disproportionately large effect on the community, and whose removal can cause many other species to disappear. An example is the starfish Pisaster, whose removal led to the loss of many invertebrate species in the intertidal zone.
keyPoints: Its removal causes loss of other species
questions.explanation: Keystone predators maintain species diversity.

questions.q: How do invasive alien species threaten native biodiversity? Give examples.
questions.answer: Alien species compete with native species for resources, prey on them or bring diseases, so the native species decline or become extinct. Examples are the Nile perch in Lake Victoria, the African catfish Clarias gariepinus, and weeds such as Lantana, Parthenium and water hyacinth.
keyPoints: Compete with or prey on native species
Examples: Nile perch, Clarias, Lantana, water hyacinth
questions.explanation: Alien species invasion is a major cause of biodiversity loss.
